title: Three bodies
hook: the Buddha as the truth body, the bliss body and the body that appears in the world

segments.voice: Yesterday, Buddha-nature: gold under the muck, a statue wrapped in rags. Your line: covered, not lost.

A monk named Vakkali is sick in bed, with one wish: to see the Buddha with his own eyes one more time. Word is sent, and the Buddha comes and sits by him. Vakkali tries to get up; the Buddha tells him to lie still. Then, instead of a soft word, a sharp question: why do you want to see this foul body? Whoever sees the teaching, he says, sees me. Whoever sees me sees the teaching. That line is in the Pali texts, and later Buddhists built a whole picture of the Buddha around it.
screen: `A SICK MONK'S WISH.` → `WHY SEE THIS BODY?` → `WHO SEES THE TEACHING SEES ME.`

segments.voice: In the Mahayana, the question of what a Buddha is grows into a three-part answer: trikaya, three bodies. Body here means something closer to a form, a way of being present. First, the truth body, the dharmakaya: the Buddha as truth itself, what was seen on the night of awakening. No edges, no birthday, no address. When the Buddha told Vakkali that whoever sees the teaching sees him, Mahayana readers heard this body. Second, the bliss body, the sambhogakaya: the Buddha as the Mahayana sutras describe him in glory, radiant, teaching great bodhisattvas in pure lands, beyond ordinary sight. Some Tibetan and East Asian practices picture the Buddha this way. Third, the body that appears, the nirmanakaya: the Buddha who is born, walks the roads, eats rice, falls ill and dies, the life this path followed in its stories. Here the human life is real, and it is also the truth taking a form people could meet and follow. Some teachers use the moon: the moon itself, its light, and its reflection in a bowl of water. One moon, met three ways. Schools explain the three bodies differently, and the teaching in this form is Mahayana; Theravada Buddhists speak of the Buddha's life and of the teaching he left, without the three-body scheme. So where is the Buddha now? In the teaching, for anyone who sees it. In forms suited to whoever is looking. And in a life once lived on real roads.
screen: `THE TRUTH BODY: DHARMAKAYA.` · `THE BLISS BODY: SAMBHOGAKAYA.` · `THE BODY THAT APPEARS: NIRMANAKAYA.` · then, large: `ONE MOON, MET THREE WAYS.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind someone who matters to you and isn't in the room, and notice three ways they're present anyway. What they stand for, the thing they taught you; how they appear in your mind's eye, a laugh, a way of standing in a doorway; and one real moment when you were actually together. Rest with all three, then let them go and come back to the breath.
Trikaya. Three bodies: the Buddha as the truth itself, as the bliss body in glory, and as the body that appears in the world. Today's word.
Your line: three bodies. Truth, glory, and a life on real roads. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: Mahayana teachers in Tibet and East Asia use the three bodies to explain how the Buddha is present: in the teaching, in visions and pure lands, and in the human life told in the Buddha's story.

chat.says: If the Buddha died long ago, where do Mahayana Buddhists say he is now?
options: In the teaching, in forms suited to whoever looks, and in a life once lived.
Reborn as an ordinary person somewhere, living a brand-new life.
Waiting in a heaven to be born again as the next Buddha.
chat.meaning: Trikaya: the truth body is met in the teaching, the bliss body appears in glory, and the body that appears lived on real roads.

trikaya.meaning: three bodies: three ways a Buddha is present

dharmakaya.meaning: the truth body: the Buddha as truth itself

sambhogakaya.meaning: the bliss body: the Buddha in glory, in pure lands

nirmanakaya.meaning: the body that appears: the Buddha born in the world

Vakkali.meaning: a sick monk who longed to see the Buddha once more

sources.ref: Mahayanasutralamkara, on the three bodies of a Buddha

notes: Vakkali (SN 22.87) is paraphrased, not quoted: the Buddha asks why he wants to see this 'foul/putrid body' and says whoever sees the Dhamma sees him, and whoever sees him sees the Dhamma. The later part of the sutta (Vakkali's death) is left out deliberately.

The moon image (moon, light, reflection) is attributed only to 'some teachers'; confirm it is a recognized teaching image for the three bodies, or replace it (a Tibetan image is sky, clouds and rain).

'Theravada Buddhists speak of the Buddha's life and of the teaching he left, without the three-body scheme': confirm fair; some Pali texts use dhammakaya (e.g. DN 27) and a Keeper may want that named.
Source for the three-body scheme given as the Mahayanasutralamkara; a Keeper may prefer another text (e.g. the Suvarnaprabhasa).

Editor: 'this body, which is going to rot' changed to 'this foul body' (closer to SN 22.87's putikaya); 'the life this path followed last year' changed to 'in its stories' (the life story was told in year one, not last year). Vakkali was also used on days 351 and 1042; kept here because the angle (the three bodies) is new.
